slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **causes** of 1919, the **programme**, **Chauri Chaura** and the **impact**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the three causes of 1919, the programme, the spread of the movement, the Chauri Chaura incident and the impact of Non-Cooperation

slides.narration: In the years after the First World War, the freedom struggle changed its character. Under Gandhiji, millions of ordinary people joined it for the first time. In this part we study three events of nineteen nineteen that led to the Non-Cooperation Movement, the programme of the movement, the incident at Chauri Chaura that ended it, and what it achieved.

slides.narration: This timeline shows the whole chapter. Non-Cooperation began in nineteen twenty and was suspended in nineteen twenty-two. Civil Disobedience began with the Dandi March in nineteen thirty and was withdrawn in nineteen thirty-four. The Quit India Resolution came in nineteen forty-two. Keep these three movements and their dates clearly apart.

slides.heading: Three causes of Non-Cooperation
slides.body_md: The **Khilafat** issue, the **Rowlatt Act** and **Jallianwala Bagh**.

rows: Muslim anger at the treatment of Turkey; chance for joint action
Firing on an unarmed crowd; loss of faith in British justice

visual.alt: Table of three causes of Non-Cooperation: the Khilafat issue of 1919 to 1920, the Rowlatt Act of March 1919 and the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy of 13 April 1919, with why each mattered
visual.caption: Three causes, one movement.

slides.narration: Three causes came together. Indian Muslims were angered by the treatment of Turkey and its Sultan after the war, which gave rise to the Khilafat Movement. The Rowlatt Act allowed detention without trial. And the firing at Jallianwala Bagh shook the faith of many Indians in British justice.

slides.heading: The Khilafat Movement
columns:
**The issue**

- After the war, harsh terms for **Turkey**
- Its **Sultan** was regarded as the **Caliph** by many Muslims
- Protest led by the **Ali brothers**

**Why it mattered**

- Gandhiji **supported** it
- A chance for **Hindu-Muslim unity**
- Khilafat and swaraj joined in **one programme**
slides.narration: Many Indian Muslims regarded the Sultan of Turkey as the Caliph, a religious head. When the victorious powers imposed harsh terms on Turkey after the war, the Ali brothers, Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, led a protest. Gandhiji supported them, and for a few years Hindus and Muslims worked together in one movement.

slides.heading: The Rowlatt Act, 1919
slides.body_md: **Detention without trial** led to a **nationwide hartal**.

visual.alt: Flow: in March 1919 the Rowlatt Act is passed, allowing detention without trial; Gandhiji calls for satyagraha; a nationwide hartal is held on 6 April 1919; protests follow in Punjab and elsewhere
visual.caption: From a law to a protest.

slides.narration: In March nineteen nineteen the government passed the Rowlatt Act, which allowed people to be arrested and held in prison without a trial. Indians felt this took away a basic right. Gandhiji called for satyagraha, and on the sixth of April shops and offices across India closed in a hartal.

slides.heading: Jallianwala Bagh, 13 April 1919
slides.body_md: An **unarmed crowd** fired upon in an **enclosed** garden at **Amritsar**.

visual.alt: Table of facts about Jallianwala Bagh: 13 April 1919, Baisakhi day, at Amritsar; General Reginald Dyer in command; the Hunter Committee inquiry; Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood
visual.caption: Estimates of the dead differ widely; we give no single figure.

slides.narration: On the Baisakhi day of thirteenth April nineteen nineteen, a crowd had gathered in the walled garden of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. Troops under General Dyer entered and fired on them. Hundreds were killed, though the estimates differ widely. Rabindranath Tagore gave up his knighthood in protest, and the Hunter Committee was appointed to inquire.

slides.body_md: Explain how **three events of 1919–20** led to Non-Cooperation.
bullets: Step 1: name **three different** causes.
Step 2: give **one detail** for each (a date, a name, a feature).
Step 3: link each to the **decision** to stop cooperating.

Firing on an unarmed crowd; loss of faith in British justice

visual.caption: Three causes, one movement.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a three-mark answer on the causes. First, choose three different causes: the Khilafat issue, the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh. Next, add one detail to each, such as the date of the firing or the feature of the Act. Finally, show how each one pushed Gandhiji towards non-cooperation.

slides.heading: The programme of Non-Cooperation
slides.body_md: **Boycott** what is British; **build** what is Indian.

rows: Surrender of titles and honorary posts
Boycott of government schools and colleges
Boycott of councils and foreign goods

visual.alt: Table of the Non-Cooperation programme: boycott items such as surrender of titles, boycott of government schools, law courts, councils and foreign goods; constructive items such as national schools, khadi and the charkha, panchayats, Hindu-Muslim unity and removing untouchability
visual.caption: Approved at Calcutta (September 1920), confirmed at Nagpur (December 1920).

slides.narration: The Congress approved the programme at a special session in Calcutta in September nineteen twenty and confirmed it at Nagpur in December. The boycott side asked people to give up titles and to leave government schools, courts and councils, and to reject foreign goods. The constructive side built national schools, khadi, panchayats and unity.

slides.heading: Quick check: build or boycott?
slides.body_md: Which action fits the **constructive** side of the programme?
slides.narration: Ask whether each action refuses something British or builds something Indian.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sorting actions
slides.body_md: Sort four **imagined** actions of 1921.
bullets: A **boycott** item **refuses** a British institution, title or product.
A **constructive** item **builds** an Indian alternative.
Write the category **and** the reason.

rows: A lawyer closes his practice in the British courts
A town opens a national school
A family burns its foreign cloth
A village sets up a panchayat to settle quarrels

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting four imagined actions of 1921: closing a law practice and burning foreign cloth are boycott items; opening a national school and setting up a panchayat are constructive items
visual.caption: Imagined actions written by SOYL. Ask: does it refuse, or does it build?

slides.narration: Let us sort four imagined actions from nineteen twenty-one. A lawyer closing his practice in the British courts and a family burning foreign cloth are refusing something, so they are boycott items. A town opening a national school and a village setting up a panchayat are building something Indian, so they are constructive items.

slides.heading: The movement spreads
slides.body_md: **Students**, **lawyers**, **peasants** and **workers** joined; **khadi** became a symbol.

rows: Surrender of titles and honorary posts
Boycott of government schools and colleges
Boycott of councils and foreign goods

visual.alt: Table of the Non-Cooperation programme: boycott items such as surrender of titles, boycott of government schools, law courts, councils and foreign goods; constructive items such as national schools, khadi and the charkha, panchayats, Hindu-Muslim unity and removing untouchability
visual.caption: Approved at Calcutta (September 1920), confirmed at Nagpur (December 1920).

slides.narration: Between nineteen twenty and nineteen twenty-two the movement spread across India. Students left government colleges, some lawyers gave up their practice, and foreign cloth was burnt in public. Peasants and workers took part in many regions. For the first time the freedom struggle reached the villages on a large scale.

slides.heading: Chauri Chaura, February 1922
slides.body_md: Violence at **Chauri Chaura**; the movement is **suspended**.

nodes.label: Police station set on fire; policemen killed
Gandhiji: the struggle must stay non-violent
Some leaders disagree; Swaraj Party formed later

visual.alt: Flow: violence at Chauri Chaura on 5 February 1922, a police station set on fire and policemen killed; Gandhiji holds that the struggle must stay non-violent; the Bardoli resolution suspends the movement; some leaders disagree and later form the Swaraj Party
visual.caption: Why the movement stopped.

slides.narration: On the fifth of February nineteen twenty-two, at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district, a crowd clashed with the police and set fire to the police station, and policemen died. Gandhiji held that the struggle had to remain non-violent, and the Congress Working Committee at Bardoli suspended the movement.

slides.heading: Quick check: the resolution
slides.body_md: The resolution that suspended the movement is named after which place?
slides.narration: The violence happened in one place, but the decision was taken in another. Which?

slides.heading: Impact of Non-Cooperation
slides.body_md: A **mass movement**, with **gains** and **limits**.

rows: Swaraj was not won within a year
People lost the fear of jail
Hindu-Muslim unity faded after the Khilafat issue ended
Violence at Chauri Chaura showed the need for discipline

visual.alt: Table of the impact of Non-Cooperation: gains such as making the Congress a mass organisation, removing the fear of jail and spreading khadi and national education; limits such as swaraj not won within a year, unity fading after the Khilafat issue, and the lesson of Chauri Chaura
visual.caption: Weigh both columns in a 4-mark answer.

slides.narration: Although it was suspended, the movement changed Indian politics. The Congress became a mass organisation, people lost their fear of jail, and khadi and national education spread. But swaraj was not won within a year as promised, and the unity of the Khilafat years did not last. Weigh both sides in an answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: non-violence
slides.body_md: True or false: Non-Cooperation was planned as an armed uprising.
slides.narration: Think about why Gandhiji stopped the movement after Chauri Chaura.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the causes of 1919, the programme approved in 1920 at Calcutta and Nagpur, the spread of boycott and constructive work, Chauri Chaura and the Bardoli resolution in 1922, and the impact as a mass movement
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Three causes came together in nineteen nineteen. The programme of boycott and constructive work was approved in nineteen twenty. The movement spread widely until violence at Chauri Chaura led to its suspension in nineteen twenty-two. Its lasting result was a mass national movement.

bullets: Keep the **three causes** separate: Khilafat, Rowlatt, Jallianwala Bagh.
Give the dates **13 April 1919** and **5 February 1922** correctly.
Sort programme items into **boycott** and **constructive**.
In impact answers, give **gains and a limit**.

Cause and effect in three short sentences
Two gains, one limit, one judgement

slides.narration: In nineteen twenty-seven the government appointed a commission under John Simon to review the working of the reforms. Not one of its members was Indian. When it arrived in nineteen twenty-eight it was met with protests and black flags. Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi charge at Lahore and died soon after.

slides.heading: Lahore, 1929: Purna Swaraj
slides.body_md: **Complete independence** becomes the goal.

rows: Working Committee authorised to start civil disobedience

visual.alt: Table of facts about the Lahore session: December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, declared Purna Swaraj, fixed 26 January 1930 as Independence Day and authorised civil disobedience

slides.narration: At the Lahore session in December nineteen twenty-nine, under Jawaharlal Nehru, the Congress declared complete independence, Purna Swaraj, as its goal. The twenty-sixth of January nineteen thirty was observed as Independence Day, and the Working Committee was authorised to begin civil disobedience.

sections.heading: 1. Causes of the Non-Cooperation Movement
sections.body_md:
- **Khilafat Movement (1919–24):** many Indian Muslims protested against the harsh peace terms imposed on **Turkey**, whose **Sultan** they regarded as the **Caliph**. The **Ali brothers** (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) led it; Gandhiji supported it.
- **Rowlatt Act (March 1919):** permitted **arrest without warrant** and **imprisonment without trial**. Gandhiji called for **satyagraha**; a nationwide **hartal** was held on **6 April 1919**.
- **Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919):** troops under **General Dyer** opened fire on an unarmed gathering in a walled garden at **Amritsar** on Baisakhi day; hundreds died, with estimates differing widely. The **Hunter Committee** inquired; **Tagore** returned his knighthood.

key_terms.definition_md: Gandhiji's method of non-violent resistance based on truth.
A general closure of shops and work as a protest.

rows: Muslim anger at the treatment of Turkey; chance for joint action
Firing on an unarmed crowd; loss of faith in British justice

- **Boycott side:** give up **titles** and honorary posts; leave **government schools and colleges**; boycott **law courts**, the **councils** and **foreign goods**.
- **Constructive side:** **national schools and colleges**; **khadi** and the **charkha**; **panchayats**; **Hindu-Muslim unity**; work against **untouchability**.

sections.heading: 3. Suspension and impact of Non-Cooperation
sections.body_md:
- **Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922),** Gorakhpur district: a crowd burnt the police station and policemen died.
- Gandhiji insisted on **non-violence**; the **Bardoli** resolution of the Working Committee **suspended** the movement. **C. R. Das** and **Motilal Nehru** later formed the **Swaraj Party** (1923).
- **Impact:** the Congress turned into a **mass organisation**; fear of the government and of jail declined; **khadi** and **national education** spread. **Limits:** swaraj was not won within a year, and unity faded after the Khilafat issue ended.

sections.heading: 4. Causes of Civil Disobedience and the Dandi March
sections.body_md:
- **Simon Commission:** appointed in **1927**, it had **no Indian member**; it was boycotted on arrival in **1928**. (Its clauses are not in the syllabus.)

- **Programme:** making salt; boycott and **picketing**; **non-payment of taxes** and breaking **forest laws** in some areas; resignations.

sections.body_md:
- **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931):** release of prisoners not charged with violence, withdrawal of ordinances, salt for personal use near the coast; the Congress to suspend the movement and go to London.
- **Second Round Table Conference (London, 1931):** Gandhiji was the **sole Congress representative**; no agreement on the **representation of minorities**.
- **Renewal (January 1932):** arrests and bans under **Lord Willingdon**; the movement was **withdrawn in 1934**.

**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up **6 April 1919** (hartal) with **13 April 1919** (Jallianwala Bagh), and **6 April 1930** (Dandi).

- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two clear points.
- 10 marks (3 + 3 + 4): facts for (i), explanation for (ii), and for (iii) a balanced evaluation with a judgement.

**8 August 1942**, **Gowalia Tank, Bombay**; slogan **Do or Die**.

cards.front_md: Why did Quit India continue after 9 August?

questions.stem_md: The Khilafat Movement in India (1919–24) was mainly concerned with which issue?

options.text_md: The partition of Bengal into two provinces
The treatment of the Ottoman Sultan, regarded as the Caliph, and of Turkey after the First World War
The demand for separate electorates in provincial councils
The price of salt in British India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The treatment of the Ottoman Sultan, regarded as the Caliph, and of Turkey after the First World War. Indian Muslims who joined the Khilafat Movement protested against the harsh treatment of Turkey and of its Sultan, whom they regarded as the Caliph. Partition, separate electorates and salt belong to other episodes.

questions.stem_md: Which two brothers are best known as leaders of the Khilafat Movement?

options.text_md: C. R. Das and J. M. Sen Gupta

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali. The Ali brothers led the Khilafat Committee and joined hands with Gandhiji. The Nehrus were father and son; Das and Sen Gupta were Bengal leaders; the Patels were brothers but not Khilafat leaders.

questions.stem_md: Which provision of the Rowlatt Act of 1919 caused the widest anger in India?

options.text_md: Persons could be arrested and kept in prison without a trial
Indians were given a majority in the councils
Salt could be made freely by anyone
Indian judges could try British subjects

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Persons could be arrested and kept in prison without a trial. The Act gave the government power to detain people without trial and to hold trials without the usual safeguards. The other options are either unrelated or the opposite of what the Act did.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined story set in 1919, a printer in Lahore is picked up by the police and held for months without any case being heard in court. Under which law of that year could this have happened?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Rowlatt Act. Detention without trial was the feature of the Rowlatt Act passed in March 1919. The Vernacular Press Act was of 1878, the Indian Councils Act of 1909, and the 1935 Act came much later.

questions.stem_md: On what date did the firing at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar take place?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 13 April 1919. The firing took place on 13 April 1919, the day of the Baisakhi festival. 6 April 1919 was the day of the nationwide hartal against the Rowlatt Act; the other dates belong to the Dandi March and the Quit India Resolution.

questions.stem_md: Which committee did the government appoint to inquire into the disturbances in Punjab, including the firing at Jallianwala Bagh?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Hunter Committee. The Hunter Committee was appointed in 1919 to look into the Punjab disturbances. The Simon Commission (1927), the Cripps Mission (1942) and the Cabinet Mission (1946) had other purposes.

questions.stem_md: Which poet gave up the knighthood conferred on him by the British government in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rabindranath Tagore. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest. The other poets are famous, but this act of protest is associated with Tagore.

questions.stem_md: The Congress approved the Non-Cooperation programme at a special session in 1920 and confirmed it at its annual session later that year. Which pair of places is correct?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Calcutta (September) and Nagpur (December). The special session at Calcutta in September 1920 accepted the programme, and the Nagpur session in December 1920 confirmed it. Lahore 1929, Lucknow 1916, Surat 1907 and Bombay 1942 belong to other events.

questions.stem_md: Sort these actions of 1920–21. Which one belongs to the boycott (negative) side of the Non-Cooperation programme?

options.text_md: Lawyers giving up practice in the British law courts
Opening a national school in a town
Spinning yarn on the charkha at home

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Lawyers giving up practice in the British law courts. Giving up the government courts is a boycott item. National schools, the charkha and panchayats are constructive items that built Indian alternatives.

questions.stem_md: A village group in 1921 decides to do something that builds rather than boycotts. Which action fits the constructive (positive) side of the Non-Cooperation programme?

options.text_md: Returning a title given by the government
Refusing to attend a government function
Withdrawing children from a government school

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Promoting khadi and hand-spinning. Promoting khadi was constructive. Returning titles, avoiding government functions and leaving government schools were boycott items.

questions.stem_md: Kamala, a character in an imagined story set in 1921, leaves her government-run college and joins a newly opened national college. Which programme was she following?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Non-Cooperation Movement. Leaving government institutions for national ones was part of the Non-Cooperation programme of 1920–22. The 1905 Swadeshi Movement came earlier and the other two came later.

questions.stem_md: Chauri Chaura, where a police station was set on fire in February 1922, is in which present-day State?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Uttar Pradesh (Gorakhpur district). Chauri Chaura is in the Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh. Amritsar, Navsari (near Dandi) and Champaran are linked with other events.

questions.stem_md: Why did Gandhiji call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922?

options.text_md: The British had granted complete independence
The Khilafat leaders had asked him to join the councils
The Simon Commission had accepted Indian demands
A crowd had turned violent at Chauri Chaura, and he held that the movement must stay non-violent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A crowd had turned violent at Chauri Chaura, and he held that the movement must stay non-violent. The violence at Chauri Chaura went against his principle of non-violence, so he suspended the movement (the Bardoli resolution of the Congress Working Committee followed). The other options did not happen.

questions.stem_md: After the suspension of Non-Cooperation, which two leaders formed the Swaraj Party to contest elections to the councils?

options.text_md: Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal
Subhas Chandra Bose and Jawaharlal Nehru
C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru. C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party in 1923 to work from inside the councils. Tilak had died in 1920; the other pairs were not its founders.

questions.stem_md: Which observation best supports the view that Non-Cooperation turned the national movement into a mass movement?

options.text_md: The Congress held its sessions in December every year
Peasants, workers, students and women in many regions took part, not only educated townspeople
Some leaders later formed a new party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Peasants, workers, students and women in many regions took part, not only educated townspeople. A mass movement means wide participation across classes and regions, which is what Non-Cooperation brought. Annual sessions, committees and a new party do not show mass participation.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Congress boycott the Simon Commission when it arrived in India in 1928?

options.text_md: All its members were British; no Indian had been included
It had come to announce independence
It was led by Gandhiji himself
It wanted to abolish the salt tax

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** All its members were British; no Indian had been included. The Commission, set up in 1927 to review the working of the reforms, had no Indian member, which Indians took as an insult. The other options are false.

questions.stem_md: Who presided over the Lahore session of the Congress in December 1929, where Purna Swaraj was adopted as the goal?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Jawaharlal Nehru. Jawaharlal Nehru presided at Lahore in 1929. Motilal Nehru had presided at Calcutta in 1928; Bose and Patel presided over later sessions.

questions.stem_md: Following the Lahore resolution, which day was observed across India as Independence Day for the first time?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 26 January 1930. The first Independence Day was observed on 26 January 1930. 31 December 1929 was when the flag was hoisted at Lahore; 6 April 1930 was the day the salt law was broken at Dandi.

questions.stem_md: From where did Gandhiji begin the Salt March on 12 March 1930?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad. The march began at Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad and ended at Dandi on the coast. The other places are linked with other phases of his work.

questions.stem_md: Why did salt make an effective symbol for starting the Civil Disobedience Movement?

options.text_md: Salt was produced only in Bombay
Salt was a luxury item bought by a few
Every household needed salt, so a tax on it touched rich and poor alike and was easy to break openly
The British had already removed the salt tax

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Every household needed salt, so a tax on it touched rich and poor alike and was easy to break openly. Because everyone used salt, the tax on it was felt by all, and making salt from sea water was a simple, visible way to break the law. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best brings out the main difference between Civil Disobedience and Non-Cooperation?

options.text_md: Civil Disobedience was violent; Non-Cooperation was peaceful
Only Non-Cooperation had a constructive programme
Civil Disobedience asked people to break chosen laws; Non-Cooperation asked them to stop cooperating with the government
Civil Disobedience was limited to Punjab

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Civil Disobedience asked people to break chosen laws; Non-Cooperation asked them to stop cooperating with the government. Civil Disobedience went further by deliberately breaking laws such as the salt law; Non-Cooperation mainly withdrew cooperation. Both were meant to be non-violent and both spread widely.

questions.stem_md: The Khudai Khidmatgars, who joined Civil Disobedience in the North-West Frontier Province, were led by
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan. Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan led the Khudai Khidmatgars, a non-violent organisation of the Frontier region. The others were national leaders in other roles.

questions.stem_md: In which month and year did Gandhiji and Lord Irwin sign their agreement?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** March 1931. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931. March 1930 was the start of the Dandi March; December 1931 the end of the Second Round Table Conference.

questions.stem_md: Under the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, what did the government agree to do?

options.text_md: Grant India complete independence at once
Release political prisoners not charged with violence
Hand over the railways to the Congress

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Release political prisoners not charged with violence. Release of political prisoners who had not used violence was one of the government's promises in the Pact, along with withdrawing ordinances and permitting salt-making for home use on the coast. Independence, ending the Viceroy's post and handing over railways were never part of it.

questions.stem_md: Who was the only representative of the Congress at the Second Round Table Conference in London in 1931?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhiji attended as the sole Congress representative. The Congress did not attend the first conference.

questions.stem_md: On which question did the Second Round Table Conference mainly break down?

options.text_md: Whether the Viceroy should live in Delhi
How minority communities were to be represented in the new constitution
The design of the national flag
The date of the next general election in Britain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** How minority communities were to be represented in the new constitution. The talks failed mainly over the representation of minorities, on which no agreement could be reached. The other options were not the issue.

questions.stem_md: An imagined diary entry from January 1932 reads: "Bapu is back from London with nothing. Today he and many others were arrested, and the Congress has been declared unlawful." Which development does it describe?

options.text_md: The renewal of Civil Disobedience after the Second Round Table Conference

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The renewal of Civil Disobedience after the Second Round Table Conference. On his return in December 1931 the movement was renewed; the government, under Lord Willingdon, arrested leaders and banned the Congress in January 1932. The other events fall in 1920, 1922 and 1942.

questions.stem_md: In which year did the Cripps Mission come to India?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1942. The Cripps Mission came in March 1942. 1939 was the start of the Second World War, 1946 the Cabinet Mission and 1928 the Simon Commission.

questions.stem_md: Where was the Quit India Resolution passed on 8 August 1942?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** At Gowalia Tank in Bombay. The All India Congress Committee passed the resolution at Gowalia Tank (now August Kranti Maidan) in Bombay. Wardha was where the Working Committee had drafted it earlier.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Japanese advance of 1942 add urgency to the demand that the British should leave India?

options.text_md: Japan had promised to grant India independence
Japan had joined the Indian National Congress
Japanese forces had reached Burma, and many felt that India could defend itself better if it were free
The British had already left Burma peacefully

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Japanese forces had reached Burma, and many felt that India could defend itself better if it were free. With Japan at Burma, near India's borders, leaders argued that a free India would defend itself with more strength than a subject one. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: The top Congress leaders were arrested early on 9 August 1942, yet protests spread across India. What best explains this?

options.text_md: The government asked the people to protest
People acted on their own, and leaders who escaped arrest guided the movement from hiding
The movement had been planned to last only one day
The Muslim League led the protests

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** People acted on their own, and leaders who escaped arrest guided the movement from hiding. With the leaders in jail, the movement became spontaneous; ordinary people and underground leaders kept it going. The other options are false.

questions.stem_md: During Quit India, people set up their own parallel governments for a time in some areas. Which group of places is correct?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. Parallel governments were set up in Ballia (UP), Tamluk (Bengal) and Satara (Maharashtra). The other places are linked with other events.

questions.stem_md: Who hoisted the national flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 August 1942 after the leaders had been arrested?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Aruna Asaf Ali. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag and became a symbol of the movement. Annie Besant had died in 1933; the others played different roles.

questions.stem_md: The Congress Working Committee resolution that suspended Non-Cooperation in February 1922 is named after which place?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Bardoli. The Working Committee met at Bardoli and passed the resolution suspending the movement. Chauri Chaura was the place of the violence.

questions.stem_md: Gandhiji left Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 and reached Dandi on 5 April 1930. About how many days was the march?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 24 days. From 12 March to 5 April is 19 days of March plus 5 of April, that is 24 days. The salt law was broken the next morning, 6 April.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Rowlatt Act of 1919 was opposed across India.

**Reason (R):** It allowed the government to keep people in prison without a trial.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: detention without trial took away a basic safeguard, which is why the Act was resisted with a nationwide hartal.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gandhiji called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922.

**Reason (R):** He believed that India had already won swaraj by then.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: he called it off because of the violence at Chauri Chaura, not because swaraj had been won.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Congress boycotted the Simon Commission.

**Reason (R):** The Commission did not include a single Indian member.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the all-British membership was seen as an insult, so the Commission was met with protests and boycott.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The salt tax was felt only by the rich, who bought salt in large quantities.

**Reason (R):** Salt was a daily necessity used by every household.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the tax fell on everyone, and the poor felt it most. R is true, and it is exactly why salt was chosen as a symbol.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Congress did not take part in the First Round Table Conference.

**Reason (R):** Gandhiji attended the Second Round Table Conference as the only Congress representative.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the Congress stayed away from the first conference because Civil Disobedience was in progress; R describes the second conference.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Quit India Movement continued even after the main Congress leaders were jailed.

**Reason (R):** Ordinary people organised protests on their own, and some leaders guided the movement from hiding.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the movement became spontaneous and was kept alive by local and underground leadership.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Non-Cooperation Movement was planned as an armed uprising against British rule.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. It was planned as a non-violent movement of non-cooperation; that is why Gandhiji suspended it when violence broke out.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A Congress member reading the news in November 1930 would have found no Congress delegate at the Round Table Conference then meeting in London.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Congress boycotted the First Round Table Conference (1930–31) because Civil Disobedience was going on.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Quit India Resolution was passed on 8 August 1942.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The leaders were arrested early the next morning, 9 August 1942.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, a family living near the sea could make salt for its own use.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Pact allowed people in coastal areas to make salt for personal use, though the salt tax itself remained.

questions.stem_md: The troops who fired on the gathering at Jallianwala Bagh were commanded by General ___.
questions.solution_md: General Reginald Dyer ordered the firing on 13 April 1919.

questions.stem_md: At its Lahore session in 1929 the Congress declared ___ (complete independence) as its goal.
questions.solution_md: The Lahore session declared Purna Swaraj as the goal.

questions.stem_md: The two-word slogan given to the people at the time of the Quit India Resolution was "___".
questions.solution_md: The slogan was Do or Die (Karo ya Maro).

questions.stem_md: Match each event of Gandhiji's mass movements with its year.

options.text_md: Agreement between Gandhiji and Lord Irwin

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Jallianwala Bagh 1919; Chauri Chaura 1922; Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931; Quit India Resolution 1942.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps of the Civil Disobedience phase in the correct order.

options.text_md: Gandhiji walks to Dandi and breaks the salt law
The movement is renewed after the London conference
Gandhiji and Lord Irwin sign a pact
Purna Swaraj is declared at Lahore

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Simon boycott (1928), Lahore (1929), Dandi (1930), the Pact (1931), renewal (1932).

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two reasons why the Khilafat question helped bring about the Non-Cooperation Movement.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons linking the Khilafat issue to the movement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Indian Muslims were angered by the harsh terms imposed on **Turkey** and its **Sultan-Caliph** after the war.
2. Gandhiji saw a chance to unite **Hindus and Muslims** in one non-violent movement, so the Khilafat and swaraj demands were joined.

marking_scheme.step: Anger at the treatment of Turkey

questions.stem_md: Mention two features of the Rowlatt Act that Indians objected to.
questions.solution_md: Any two features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A person could be **arrested without a warrant** and **detained without trial**.
2. Cases could be heard **without the usual right of appeal**, by special courts, which Indians saw as a denial of justice.

questions.stem_md: Give two ways in which the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy affected the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Two effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It turned many **moderate Indians** against British rule and destroyed faith in British **justice**.
2. It led to protests such as **Tagore** giving up his **knighthood**, and it prepared the ground for **Non-Cooperation**.

questions.stem_md: Name any two boycott items in the programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
questions.solution_md: Any two boycott items.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Boycott of **government schools and colleges**.
2. Boycott of **law courts** by lawyers and litigants. (Also: surrender of **titles**, boycott of **councils** and of **foreign goods**.)

questions.stem_md: Name any two constructive items in the programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
questions.solution_md: Any two constructive items.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Setting up **national schools and colleges**.
2. Popularising **khadi** and the **charkha**. (Also: **panchayats** for disputes, **Hindu-Muslim unity**, removal of **untouchability**.)

questions.stem_md: Why did Gandhiji suspend Non-Cooperation even though it was at its height in early 1922?
questions.solution_md: The event and the principle behind the decision.

answer.model_answer_md: At **Chauri Chaura** (5 February 1922) a crowd set fire to a police station and policemen died. Gandhiji held that the people were **not yet ready** for **non-violent** struggle, so he stopped the movement rather than let it turn violent.

questions.stem_md: Point out two lasting effects of the Non-Cooperation Movement, even though it was suspended.
questions.solution_md: Two lasting effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It made the Congress a **mass organisation** with members in **villages** and towns.
2. People lost their **fear** of the government and of jail, and **khadi** and **national education** took root.

questions.stem_md: How did the reaction to the Simon Commission prepare the ground for Civil Disobedience?
questions.solution_md: Protest against the Commission and its effect.

answer.model_answer_md: The **all-British** Commission was met with protests wherever it went. The anger, and the lathi charge in which **Lala Lajpat Rai** was injured, united parties and pushed the Congress towards a **stronger demand** and a new **struggle**.

marking_scheme.step: Pushed the Congress towards a new struggle

questions.stem_md: Mention two decisions associated with the Lahore session of the Congress (1929).
questions.solution_md: Any two decisions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence) was declared the **goal**.
2. **26 January 1930** was to be observed as **Independence Day**, and the Working Committee was authorised to start **civil disobedience**.

questions.stem_md: Explain two reasons why the Dandi March is remembered as a turning point.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons for its significance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It turned a simple act, **making salt**, into a **mass protest** that anyone could join.
2. It drew **national and world attention** and launched **Civil Disobedience** across India.

marking_scheme.step: Mass participation through a simple act
Attention and launch of the movement

questions.stem_md: State two terms of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931.
questions.solution_md: Any two terms.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The government would **release political prisoners** not charged with violence.
2. The Congress would **suspend Civil Disobedience** and attend the **Second Round Table Conference**. (Also: salt-making allowed for **personal use** near the coast.)

questions.stem_md: Why was Civil Disobedience renewed in 1932?
questions.solution_md: Failure in London and the government's repression.

answer.model_answer_md: Gandhiji returned from the **Second Round Table Conference** with **no agreement**, and the new Viceroy **Lord Willingdon** met the Congress with **arrests** and **bans**. With talks failed, the movement was **resumed** in January 1932.

questions.stem_md: How did the failure of the Cripps Mission lead to the Quit India Movement?
questions.solution_md: Why the offer failed and what followed.

answer.model_answer_md: The Mission's offer looked to a settlement **after the war** and did not meet the demand for **real power now**. Its failure convinced the Congress that the British would not leave willingly, so it chose a final **mass struggle**.

marking_scheme.step: Offer did not meet Indian demands
Led to a final mass struggle

questions.stem_md: Assess two reasons why the Quit India Movement is considered significant.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons, with judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It showed that the demand for **freedom** had spread to **ordinary people** everywhere, even without leaders.
2. It made it clear that the British could **not rule India much longer** against such feeling.

questions.stem_md: Explain how three events of 1919–20 together led Gandhiji to launch Non-Cooperation.
questions.solution_md: Three causes, each linked to the decision.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rowlatt Act (1919):** detention without trial showed that British rule would not respect Indian rights.
2. **Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919):** the firing on an unarmed crowd shattered faith in British **justice**.
3. **Khilafat issue:** the treatment of **Turkey** angered Muslims, giving a chance for a **joint** Hindu-Muslim struggle.

questions.stem_md: Describe three items of the programme of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
questions.solution_md: Three programme items.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Breaking the **salt law** by making salt from sea water.
2. **Boycott** of **foreign cloth** and **picketing** of shops selling it and liquor.
3. **Non-payment of taxes** and land revenue in some areas, and breaking of **forest laws**.

marking_scheme.step: Non-payment of taxes or forest laws

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which Civil Disobedience widened the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct ways.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Women** came out in large numbers to make salt, picket shops and court arrest.
2. **Peasants** and **traders** joined through non-payment of taxes and boycott, which cut **British trade**.
3. It reached new regions, such as the **Frontier** with the **Khudai Khidmatgars**, and drew **world attention**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three causes of the Quit India Movement.
questions.solution_md: Three causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Failure of the Cripps Mission** (1942): its offer did not give real power during the war.
2. **Japanese threat:** Japan had reached **Burma**, and leaders felt a free India could defend itself better.
3. **Wartime hardship:** rising **prices** and **shortages** caused widespread discontent.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the causes of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

(i) What was the Khilafat Movement, and how did it bring Hindus and Muslims together? **[3]**
(ii) Why did Indians oppose the Rowlatt Act, and how did Gandhiji respond? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy changed Indian attitudes to British rule. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Khilafat and unity; Rowlatt and the response; the effect of Jallianwala Bagh.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) After the **First World War**, the Allies imposed harsh terms on **Turkey**, whose **Sultan** Indian Muslims regarded as the **Caliph**. The **Ali brothers** led a movement in protest, and Gandhiji supported it, so Hindus and Muslims joined in **one struggle**.

(ii) The **Rowlatt Act (March 1919)** allowed **arrest without warrant** and **detention without trial**. Gandhiji called for a **satyagraha** and a nationwide **hartal on 6 April 1919**.

(iii) On **13 April 1919** troops under **General Dyer** fired on an unarmed crowd in the enclosed **Jallianwala Bagh** at **Amritsar**; hundreds were killed, though estimates differ widely. Moderate Indians lost faith in British **justice**, **Tagore** gave up his knighthood, and the **Hunter Committee** was seen as too mild. Gandhiji concluded that **non-cooperation** with such a government was a duty.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Non-Cooperation Movement.

(i) Where and when was its programme approved and confirmed? **[3]**
(ii) List three boycott items of the programme. **[3]**
(iii) Describe four constructive items of the programme. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Approval; boycott items; constructive items.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **special session** of the Congress at **Calcutta** in **September 1920** approved the programme, and the annual session at **Nagpur** in **December 1920** confirmed it. Gandhiji led the movement and held that, if the programme were followed fully, swaraj could come within a year.

(ii) Boycott items: surrender of **titles** and honorary posts; boycott of **government schools and colleges** and of **law courts**; boycott of the **councils**, whose elections were due in 1920, and of **foreign goods**, which were burnt in public bonfires.

(iii) Constructive items: setting up **national schools** and colleges; popularising **khadi** and the **charkha**; settling disputes through **panchayats**; promoting **Hindu-Muslim unity** and working to remove **untouchability**. A fund was raised to support the work, and volunteers carried the message from town to village, so that the movement reached people who had never taken part in politics before.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the end of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

(i) What happened at Chauri Chaura in February 1922? **[3]**
(ii) Why did Gandhiji call off the movement, and how did some leaders react? **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the impact of the Non-Cooperation Movement on the freedom struggle. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Event; reason and reaction; balanced impact.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) On **5 February 1922**, at **Chauri Chaura** in the **Gorakhpur** district of the United Provinces, a crowd clashed with the police and **set fire to the police station**; a number of policemen, commonly given as 22, died.

(ii) Gandhiji believed the struggle had to stay **non-violent** and that the people were not yet ready for it, so the **Bardoli** resolution suspended the movement. Some leaders, such as **Motilal Nehru** and **C. R. Das**, felt the decision came at its height; Das and Motilal later formed the **Swaraj Party**.

(iii) The movement made the Congress a **mass organisation**, brought **peasants, workers, students and women** into politics and removed the **fear** of jail. **Khadi** and **national education** spread. Its weakness was that **Hindu-Muslim unity** did not last after the Khilafat issue ended, but it prepared the ground for later mass struggles.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the causes of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

(i) Why was the Simon Commission opposed in India? **[3]**
(ii) What did the Congress decide at its Lahore session in 1929? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how these developments led to the launch of Civil Disobedience in 1930. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Simon opposition; Lahore decisions; link to 1930.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Commission, appointed in **1927** to review the working of the reforms, had **no Indian member**. Indians saw this as an insult, and it was met with **black flags** and protests; **Lala Lajpat Rai** was injured in a lathi charge at **Lahore** in 1928 and died soon after.

(ii) Under **Jawaharlal Nehru** the Congress declared **Purna Swaraj** as its goal, decided to observe **26 January 1930** as **Independence Day**, and authorised the Working Committee to start **civil disobedience**.

(iii) With the British making no offer that met the new goal, the Congress needed a **mass struggle**. Gandhiji placed demands before the Viceroy and, when they were not accepted, chose the **salt law** as the first law to break. The **Dandi March** (12 March – 6 April 1930) launched the movement across India.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The march began at **Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad**, on **12 March 1930**, and reached **Dandi** on the coast on **5 April**; Gandhiji broke the **salt law** there on **6 April 1930**.

(ii) **Salt** was needed by **every household**, so the salt tax and the government monopoly on salt affected **rich and poor** alike. Making salt from sea water was a **simple, peaceful** act that anyone could join, which made it a powerful **symbol**.

(iii) Programme: **making salt** in defiance of the law; **boycott** of foreign cloth and **picketing** of shops selling it and liquor; **non-payment of taxes** and land revenue in some areas; breaking **forest laws** and resigning from government posts.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the years 1931–34.

(i) State three terms of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. **[3]**
(ii) Why did the Second Round Table Conference fail? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how Civil Disobedience was renewed and how it ended. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Terms; failure; renewal and end.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Signed on **5 March 1931**: the government would **release political prisoners** not charged with violence and **withdraw its ordinances**; people near the coast could **make salt for their own use**; the Congress would **suspend Civil Disobedience** and attend the **Second Round Table Conference**.

(ii) At the conference in **London** (1931) Gandhiji was the **sole Congress representative**. The talks broke down mainly over the **representation of minorities**, on which the parties could not agree, so he returned without a settlement.

(iii) On his return in **December 1931** the movement was **renewed** (January 1932). The government under **Lord Willingdon** arrested Gandhiji and other leaders, **banned** the Congress and used harsh measures. The movement gradually lost strength and was **withdrawn in 1934**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Quit India Movement.

(i) Explain three causes of the movement. **[3]**
(ii) What was decided at Bombay on 8 August 1942, and what happened the next morning? **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the significance of the movement for India's independence. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Causes; the resolution and arrests; balanced significance.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Cripps Mission** (1942) failed to offer real power during the war; **Japanese** forces had reached **Burma**, and leaders felt a free India would defend itself better; wartime **price rises** and **shortages** caused discontent.

(ii) The **All India Congress Committee** passed the **Quit India Resolution** at **Gowalia Tank** and called for a non-violent mass struggle, with the slogan **Do or Die**. Early on **9 August** the main leaders were **arrested**.

(iii) With leaders in jail, people organised **strikes and protests** on their own; **underground** leaders and a secret radio kept up the message, and **parallel governments** arose in places such as **Ballia, Tamluk and Satara**. Although the government suppressed it, the movement showed that the demand for **freedom** had reached **every class**, and it made clear that British rule could not continue for long.

questions.stem_md:
Compare Gandhiji's three mass movements.

(i) State the main aim and one method of each movement: Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India. **[3]**
(ii) How did Civil Disobedience go further than Non-Cooperation? **[3]**
(iii) In your view, which feature was common to all three, and why did it matter? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Aims and methods; how CDM went further; reasoned common feature.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Non-Cooperation (1920–22):** swaraj, by **withdrawing cooperation** (boycott of schools, courts, councils). **Civil Disobedience (1930–34):** Purna Swaraj, by **breaking chosen laws** such as the salt law. **Quit India (1942):** an immediate end of British rule, by a **mass struggle** with the slogan Do or Die.

(ii) Non-Cooperation mainly stopped cooperating; Civil Disobedience **deliberately broke laws** and refused **taxes** in some areas. It also drew far more **women** and spread to new regions.

(iii) All three relied on **mass participation** of ordinary people. This mattered because it turned the Congress into a **people's movement**, showed the British that Indians of every class wanted **freedom**, and built the confidence that made **independence** possible. (A reasoned answer naming non-violence as the common feature is also accepted.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Rowlatt Act**, which allowed detention without trial, and the firing at **Jallianwala Bagh** on 13 April 1919. Together they convinced Gandhiji that cooperation with the government was no longer possible.

(ii) The boycott of the all-British **Simon Commission** (1928) united opinion against the government, and at **Lahore** (1929) the Congress declared **Purna Swaraj** and authorised civil disobedience. This led directly to the **Dandi March** of 1930.

(iii) In **1920** the movement was led and controlled by **Gandhiji**, and he could **suspend** it after Chauri Chaura. In **1942** the leaders were **arrested** the morning after the resolution, so the movement became **spontaneous**, was led by **underground** and local leaders, and could not be called off in the same way.
